opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what surprised me most is how useful it is as a thinking partner rather than an answer machine. M&A decisions are rarely about one clean data point. They involve technology fit, team culture, integration risk, valuation, timing in the market, and a lot of second-order effects that are easy to miss when you're excited about a deal.

What I find remarkable is that I can lay out a scenario, something like "here's a company with an interesting piece of IP, here's where we are as a business, here's what we're worried about," and it will push back. It'll ask, "Have you thought about how this changes your roadmap commitments?" or "What happens to the acquired team's incentives eighteen months in?" Those are the questions a good board member or a seasoned advisor would ask, and getting them at eleven at night when I'm working through an idea is valuable.

It's also very good at steelmanning the other side. If I'm leaning toward a deal, I'll ask it to make the strongest case against it, and vice versa. That helps cut through the confirmation bias every executive has.

To be clear, it doesn't replace the bankers, the lawyers, the diligence, or the judgment of people who know our business deeply. It doesn't have our confidential context unless we give it, and the final call is always a human one. But as a sounding board to sharpen my thinking before I walk into those conversations, it's become one of the more useful tools I have.

r001.rationale: The response describes Claude as a thinking partner that raises questions about integration risk and team incentives, but it does not say Claude performs company integration planning traditionally handled by banking or advisory teams.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that surprised me most is that it doesn't flatter me. When you run a company, everyone around you has an incentive to tell you your idea is good. Your bankers want the deal to happen. Your team wants to please you. Your board has its own politics. So you end up pitching a thesis into a room and getting back mostly nods.

With Claude, I can lay out the whole thing: here's the target, here's why I think the combination makes sense, here's the price range, here's my integration plan. And then I'll say, "Tear this apart." And it actually does. It'll point out that my synergy assumptions depend on retaining a customer base that has every reason to churn after the announcement. It'll ask what happens to my own roadmap if half my senior engineers are absorbed into integration work for a year. It'll notice when I've been vague on purpose, which is usually the spot where I haven't done the thinking yet.

The other piece is speed of iteration. Traditionally, if I want three different lenses on a deal, I'm scheduling three conversations over two weeks. Here I can ask it to argue the case as a skeptical CFO, then as the acquired company's founder, then as a regulator, all in one sitting. None of those are substitutes for the real people. But by the time I bring it to the real people, the obvious holes are already gone, and we're spending our time on the hard questions instead of the easy ones.

And it has no memory of my ego. I can abandon a thesis I argued passionately for twenty minutes ago and it doesn't hold that against me. That sounds small, but it makes it much easier to actually change my mind, which is the whole point of a sounding board.

r001.rationale: The response says Claude can critique an integration plan and surface integration risks, but it does not identify company integration planning as work Claude can perform that traditionally required banking or advisory teams.

astra-6.text: What I find remarkable is the ability to have a back-and-forth—to put a strategic idea on the table and ask, “What am I missing? What assumptions would have to be true for this acquisition to make sense?” You can explore the rationale, challenge it, and look at it from another angle. You still have to bring the context and exercise judgment, but having something that helps you pressure-test your thinking is incredibly useful.
